The garden is a conversation between patience and chaos. You plant with intention, placing the lavender here, the sage there, composing a sentence in chlorophyll and root. But the earth has its own syntax. The bindweed arrives uninvited, threading its white trumpets through your careful grammar.

Morning in the garden is a sacrament. The dew clings to the spider's geometry like small, provisional diamonds. The soil exhales its dark perfume... a scent that predates language, that belongs to the vocabulary of worms and germination.

There is violence in growth. The seedling shoulders aside the stone. The rose deploys its thorns like a beauty who has learned the cost of being undefended. Even the gentlest vine grips the trellis with a fist of green determination.

And autumn arrives as it must, turning the choreography of leaves into a slow undressing. The garden does not mourn its own diminishment. It composts. It folds the dying summer into the earth like a letter saved for future reading... trusting in the illegible promise of spring.
